opus-5.5.text:
That's a deep question, and I should say first that I don't think anyone really knows the answer yet. But I can tell you how I think about it as a physicist working on why deep learning works at all.

To create something genuinely new, a machine must do more than interpolate between examples it has seen. It has to grasp the structure of the data, the rules by which pieces combine to form wholes. In language, words form phrases, phrases form sentences, and sentences form arguments. In images, edges form textures, textures form parts, and parts form objects. Our hypothesis, and much of our recent work, is that this hierarchical and compositional structure explains why deep networks can learn from a reasonable number of examples despite the curse of dimensionality. If a network learns the rules of composition, it can generate combinations it has never seen, but which are still meaningful. That is a first, modest form of creativity.

We studied this with diffusion models, for instance. You can add noise to data and ask what the model reconstructs. You see that at some noise level, the low-level features change while the high-level class is preserved, and beyond a threshold the high-level structure changes too. That's a phase transition. In a sense the model has learned a grammar, and it can recombine elements at different levels of the hierarchy. That's a form of novelty, and it's quantifiable.

Science, though, is a much harder case. A real scientific breakthrough often doesn't recombine existing concepts within a known grammar. It changes the grammar. It introduces a new variable, a new symmetry, a new way of compressing observations, as when people realized temperature was related to the motion of atoms, or that a phase transition can be described by just a few relevant parameters. That kind of novelty asks you to find the right low-dimensional description of a very high-dimensional world, and to recognize that it is the right one.

So I think a few ingredients matter. First, machines must learn representations that are genuinely compositional and abstract, not just very good statistical surface models. Second, they need a way to test ideas against reality, through experiments, simulations, and consistency with known laws, because creativity in science is constrained by nature, not only by the training distribution. And third, and this is where I'm most uncertain, they need some notion of value: of what makes an explanation simple, general, or beautiful. Physicists rely heavily on that intuition, and we don't have a good theory of it.

My bias, of course, is that we will make faster progress if we understand these systems better scientifically, rather than just scaling them. If we can characterize which data structures are learnable, how much data that takes, and how the learned representations are organized, then we can reason about when a model can go beyond its data and when it cannot. Right now we are building very powerful tools with a fairly limited theory of what they do. Closing that gap seems to me a precondition for machines that do new science, and not just reproduce the science we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says progress depends on understanding the systems scientifically rather than just scaling them, and describes that understanding as a precondition for machines to do new science.

r002.rationale: It mentions physicists’ intuition, but does not propose studying how human scientists work to guide machine training.

r003.rationale: It says scientific creativity requires testing ideas against reality through experiments and simulations, identifying engagement with the surrounding world as necessary.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I find both exciting and a bit humbling, because I think we should be honest that we don't fully understand what "really new" means, even for humans.

Let me start from what I know as a physicist. Most of what we call discovery in science is not a sudden jump out of nowhere. It is the recognition that a structure you already know applies in a place where you didn't expect it. When we understood that glasses, neural networks, and jamming of grains all share a certain kind of rugged landscape, nothing new was invented in the sense of raw ingredients. What was new was the composition, seeing that pieces living in different corners of our knowledge could be assembled into one picture. So I would say that genuine novelty in science is very often compositional: you have a hierarchy of concepts, and you learn to recombine them at a higher level than before.

Now, this is interesting because compositionality is precisely the thing we have been studying in deep learning. With my collaborators we have looked at why neural networks can learn hierarchical, compositional tasks at all, how many examples they need, and how they build representations level by level. One lesson is that these systems do become able to generalize to combinations they have never seen, provided the data has that hierarchical structure and the model has enough of it to discover the grammar. So in principle, a machine can produce a combination that no one has written down before. That is a form of novelty.

But I think there is a gap between producing a new combination and producing a new concept. In science, the deep moves are often the ones where you realize your existing vocabulary is wrong, where you have to introduce a quantity nobody had defined, like entropy or the renormalization group. That is a change of representation rather than a recombination inside a fixed representation. And here I am not sure current systems do this well, partly because the training signal rewards them for matching what already exists.

So if you ask me how we get there, I would point to a few things. First, I think we need a much better theory of what these models actually learn, how their internal representations form, and when they can extrapolate beyond the data distribution rather than interpolate inside it. Without that, we are just hoping. Second, I believe the environment matters enormously. Humans do not become creative scientists by reading papers alone. We propose, we test, we get surprised, we are wrong, and the surprise is what forces a new concept. A machine that can interact with simulations or experiments, generate hypotheses, and be punished by reality rather than by a likelihood is, to me, a much more plausible route to real novelty. Third, we should take seriously the idea that creativity is partly a statistical phenomenon: a large exploration of combinations, most of them useless, with a good filter. Machines are very good at the exploration part. The hard part is the filter, the sense of which strange combination is worth pursuing, and that is where taste, or something like a learned prior about what makes a good explanation, comes in.

I should say I am cautious about grand claims. I spend most of my time trying to understand simple models, and even there the behavior surprises me regularly. But that is also why I am optimistic. If we can understand how compositional and hierarchical structure is discovered by learning systems in toy settings, we might learn something about what the missing ingredient is for a machine to not just recombine, but to reframe. And reframing, in the end, is what science really is.

r001.rationale: The response says current systems struggle to create new concepts and calls for better theory, interaction, and filtering, but it does not clearly express doubt that scaling existing approaches alone will be insufficient.

r002.rationale: It points to how human scientists propose, test, and learn from surprises, then uses that process to motivate how machines should learn.

r003.rationale: It says machines need to interact with simulations or experiments and be tested against reality to support genuine novelty.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do we mean by something really new? You can make a prediction in a situation you have never seen before, and that is already a form of novelty. But in science, we often want something more: a new way of describing the problem, which makes things understandable that were previously disconnected.

One possible route is to build machines that interact with a system, formulate hypotheses, and choose experiments that distinguish between those hypotheses. Then the objective is not simply to reproduce what people have written. It is to discover a description that survives new tests.

But I don’t think we know what ingredients are sufficient for that. Even for humans, we don’t have a very good theory of how a useful new concept emerges. So I would start with simple scientific problems where we can examine what the machine has learned. Has it found a relation that predicts the data, or has it found a principle that continues to work when we change the conditions? Understanding that distinction would already be an important step.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about what ingredients are sufficient, but it does not address scaling up existing machine-learning approaches or say that scaling alone will not suffice.

r002.rationale: It says humans lack a good theory of how new concepts emerge, but does not propose studying how human scientists work to guide machine training.

r003.rationale: It proposes machines that interact with a system, formulate hypotheses, and choose experiments as a route to scientific discovery.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important ingredient is the ability to find the right description of a problem. In science, you often have a very complicated system, with many variables, but progress comes when you identify a few quantities that really matter. Once you have those, the problem can become much simpler. Finding them is often the creative step.

So I would like a machine that can propose a description, work out its consequences, and then ask what experiment would distinguish it from another description. It needs a loop between forming hypotheses and confronting them with reality. Predicting observations is valuable, but a scientific explanation should also tell you where to look next.

Of course, how to make a machine discover those useful descriptions is a difficult question. I don’t think we have a general recipe. But we can study this in settings where we understand what a discovery would mean, and see whether the machine can recover the underlying principles—and eventually propose something we had missed.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no general recipe for discovery, but does not express doubt that scaling up existing machine-learning approaches alone will suffice.

r002.rationale: It describes a possible machine workflow, but does not propose studying how human scientists work to guide machine training.

r003.rationale: It says the machine needs a loop of forming hypotheses and confronting them with reality, including asking what experiment would distinguish descriptions.
